analysis.one_liner: Makes pharmacy benefit managers legally accountable to health plans as fiduciaries and forces fee disclosures.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in mid-December 2025 with bipartisan backing and referred to the Senate Health Committee, which has taken no action on it yet.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are middlemen that decide which drugs employer health plans cover, negotiate secret rebates with drugmakers, and process drug claims — and they keep part of the money flowing through that system. This bill changes the federal law governing employer health plans (ERISA) so that PBMs must act as fiduciaries, meaning they are legally required to put the health plan's interests ahead of their own profits. It also requires PBMs to disclose all direct and indirect compensation they receive, and bars them from using contracts to dodge legal liability if they breach those duties.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees and families covered by employer health plans, who pay prescription drug costs through premiums and copays. Employers who sponsor those plans also gain, because clearer disclosure and a legal duty of loyalty make it harder for a PBM to quietly profit off the plan's drug spending. The changes apply to plan years starting at least 12 months after enactment [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds PBMs to the list of parties legally deemed fiduciaries under ERISA when they build drug networks, build formularies, negotiate rebates, process drug claims, or conduct utilization review for a group health plan — making them legally bound to act in the plan's interest rather than their own [S2].

It requires PBMs and third-party administrators to disclose direct and indirect compensation they expect to receive for pharmacy benefit management and claims-processing services, closing the gap that lets hidden rebates and fees go unreported to employers [S2].

It prohibits PBMs from being indemnified or otherwise shielded from liability for breaching their fiduciary duties, and voids contract terms that try to do so, so wronged plans can actually hold them accountable [S2].
It clarifies that a PBM cannot serve as the 'responsible plan fiduciary' for the disclosure requirements, preventing the middleman from controlling the plan's oversight of its own compensation [S2].

analysis.who_pays: PBMs — the large middlemen firms that currently profit from opaque rebate and spread arrangements — along with the big insurance conglomerates that own them, which would lose revenue from arrangements they can no longer keep hidden or shield with indemnification clauses [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill does not directly lower the price of any drug; its effect depends on plans using the new disclosure and fiduciary rules to renegotiate, so savings for workers are indirect and not guaranteed [S2].
It applies only to employer group health plans governed by ERISA, so people whose drug coverage runs through Medicare, Medicaid, or the individual market get no direct help from this bill [S2].

Imposing fiduciary duties, disclosure obligations, and new liability exposure on PBM services raises compliance costs for the industry, and an honest supporter should acknowledge that some of that cost could show up in the administrative fees plans pay — though the disclosure requirement is designed to make any such increase visible to employers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go to the millions of people whose drug costs run through employer plans, giving them and their employers visibility into where their drug money goes and a legal tool to demand it back. The main costs fall on PBMs and their parent companies, whose current business model depends on the opacity this bill removes. The honest caveat is that this is an accountability mechanism, not a price cap — whether workers actually see lower costs depends on employers and plans using the new tools, and the bill leaves out Medicare and Medicaid drug spending entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was just introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where no vote or hearing has happened yet.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall (R-KS) introduced the PBM FAIR Act on December 17, 2025 [S1] [S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which is the only action the bill has received so far [S4].
The bill has three cosponsors: two Senate Democrats and one Senate Republican, making its initial support bipartisan [S3].
The bill text shows it was introduced 'for himself, Mr. Kaine, Mr. Grassley, and Ms. Hassan,' meaning the cosponsors are Sens. Tim Kaine (D-VA), Chuck Grassley (R-IA), and Maggie Hassan (D-NH) [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has been decided yet. The status quo that benefits large PBMs remains fully in place while the bill sits unreferred to any vote in the HELP Committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PBMs, while the bill sits idle

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator introduced it with two Democratic and one Republican cosponsors — 2 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 55 Senate Republicans — so far there is no party split.

industries.note: PBMs currently negotiate rebates, run formularies, and process drug claims largely out of public view, keeping a slice of the money flowing through employer drug plans. This bill makes them fiduciaries legally bound to put the plan first, forces them to disclose all their compensation, and strips their ability to contract away liability — a direct hit to the opacity their business model runs on [S2].

Most of the largest PBMs sit inside big insurers, so revenue the PBM earns from hidden spreads and rebates flows to the parent company. Disclosure and fiduciary rules threaten that stream and expose the vertical integration between the plan's gatekeeper and the plan's administrator [S2].

Employers who self-fund health benefits would get required compensation disclosures and a PBM with enforceable fiduciary duties, tools to audit and renegotiate drug spending they currently cannot fully see [S2].

Manufacturers would still pay rebates, but a PBM acting as a plan fiduciary may have to route more of that money back to the plan instead of keeping it, which could change the rebate economics manufacturers have negotiated around [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The bill is one day into the 119th Congress's remaining session and sits in the HELP Committee with three cosponsors. Most Senate bills referred to committee never receive a markup or floor vote, and similar PBM accountability bills in prior Congresses advanced through hearings without becoming law. Its path depends entirely on whether the committee chair schedules action; if PBM reform stays on the agenda, it could move as part of a broader package, but on its own it is likely to sit.
